title: Continuous-variable Quantum Communication
authors: Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, And Valerio Pruneri
abstract:
Author(s): Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, and Valerio Pruneri

The quantum nature of radiation is not solely corpuscular. In the “continuous-variable” setting, the wavelike quantum properties can be observed. Quantum technologies put this continuous-variable nature of light to use, with applications in various forms of quantum information processing. This review concentrates on the developments of these wave-based techniques in quantum communication. Compared with photon-based (corpuscular) variants, the continuous-variable approach is equally well developed and has certain conceptual and practical advantages.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015003] Published Mon Mar 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of continuous-variable quantum communication, covering protocols, security, and implementations.
motivation: To provide an up-to-date overview of continuous-variable (CV) quantum communication, highlighting its advantages and recent developments.
method: The paper reviews theoretical foundations, protocols (e.g., CV-QKD), security proofs, and experimental implementations, comparing with discrete-variable approaches.
result: Summarizes the state of the art in CV quantum communication, including security proofs and practical demonstrations, and identifies future directions.
conclusion: CV quantum communication is a mature and promising field with practical advantages, and further advances are expected.

title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory, security, and photonic implementations.
motivation: To provide a structured overview of quantum cryptography beyond key distribution, highlighting the potential and limitations of quantum resources for various cryptographic tasks.
method: The paper classifies quantum cryptographic primitives, explains their security definitions and limitations, and discusses experimental implementations using photonic techniques.
result: It presents a taxonomy of quantum crypto primitives and reviews their theoretical foundations and experimental status.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers enhanced security for many tasks beyond QKD, but practical implementations face challenges; the review serves as a guide for future research.

title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: This paper develops semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof, based on generalized noncontextuality.
motivation: To provide practical tools for detecting and quantifying nonclassicality in quantum processes, complementing theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities.
method: The authors formulate semidefinite programs that serve as certificates and witnesses for nonclassicality, applicable to individual states, measurements, and sets, and demonstrate them with examples.
result: They present explicit SDP-based methods that can certify nonclassicality in various scenarios, as illustrated through examples.
conclusion: The work offers a versatile framework for nonclassicality detection, advancing the study of quantum contextuality and its applications.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: This paper connects Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks, providing new lower bounds and a magic monotone.
motivation: To understand and improve bounds on stabilizer ranks, which are crucial for quantum resource theories and magic state distillation.
method: The authors study the connection between Barnes Wall lattices and stabilizer states, derive quantitative lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity, define a new magic monotone (Barnes Wall norm), and provide a fidelity amplification algorithm.
result: They obtain the best lower bound on approximate stabilizer rank for magic states, show tight upper bounds for the new monotone, and give an elementary proof of existence of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks.
conclusion: The work advances the resource theory of magic states by providing new tools and bounds, with implications for quantum computation and information.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper provides a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, offering explicit bases and a graphical calculus, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: The Clifford group is central to quantum information, but the structure of its commutant was only partially understood for small tensor powers and qubit numbers. A complete theory is needed to unlock applications in pseudorandomness, learning, and entanglement distillation.
method: The authors derive an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant for arbitrary tensor power and qubit number, introduce an alternative basis of isotropic sums of Pauli operators, and develop a graphical calculus for manipulating these basis elements.
result: They compute the dimension of the commutant, show the basis is generated by permutations and at most three other operators, and apply the theory to characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, with an operational interpretation of stabilizer entropies.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant provides a powerful tool for quantum information, with implications for magic resource theory and property testing, and extends to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

title: Fast Quantum Measurement Tomography With Optimal Error Bounds
authors: Leonardo Zambrano, Sergi Ramos-Calderer, And Richard Kueng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2162 (2026).

We present a two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography that is light on classical co-processing cost and still achieves optimal sample complexity. Given measurement data from a known probe state ensemble, we first apply least-squares estimation to produce an unconstrained approximation of the POVM, and then project this estimate onto the set of valid quantum measurements. For a POVM with [MATH] outcomes acting on a [MATH]-dimensional system, we show that the protocol requires [MATH] samples to achieve error [MATH] in worst-case distance, and [MATH] samples in average-case distance. We further establish two matching sample complexity lower bounds of [MATH] and [MATH] for any non-adaptive, single-copy POVM tomography protocol. Hence, our projected least squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal in both the dimension and the number of outcomes for both distances. Our method admits an analytic form when using global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles and enables rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees. Finally, we also complement our findings with empirical performance studies carried out on a noisy superconducting quantum computer with flux-tunable transmon qubits.

.
tldr: This paper presents a sample-optimal two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography using projected least squares, with rigorous error bounds and experimental validation on a superconducting quantum computer.
motivation: Quantum measurement tomography is essential for characterizing quantum devices, but existing protocols often have high classical processing cost or suboptimal sample complexity. The authors aim to design a protocol that is both computationally efficient and sample-optimal.
method: The protocol first applies least-squares estimation to measurement data from known probe states, then projects the unconstrained estimate onto the set of valid POVMs. They analyze sample complexity for worst-case and average-case distances, and establish matching lower bounds for any non-adaptive single-copy protocol.
result: The protocol achieves optimal sample complexity in both dimension and number of outcomes for both distances, with analytic forms for global and local 2-designs. Empirical tests on a noisy superconducting quantum computer confirm its practical effectiveness.
conclusion: The proposed projected least squares method provides a sample-optimal and computationally light solution for quantum measurement tomography, with strong theoretical guarantees and practical viability.

title: Towards Unconditional Uncloneable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Anne Broadbent, Eric Culf, Ion Nechita, Clément Pellegrini, And Denis Rochette
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2157 (2026).

Uncloneable encryption is a cryptographic primitive which encrypts a classical message into a quantum ciphertext, such that two quantum adversaries are limited in their capacity of being able to simultaneously decrypt, given the key and quantum side-information produced from the ciphertext. Since its initial proposal and scheme in the random oracle model by Broadbent and Lord [TQC 2020], uncloneable encryption has developed into an important primitive at the foundation of quantum uncloneability for cryptographic primitives. Despite sustained efforts, however, the question of unconditional uncloneable encryption (and in particular of the simplest case, called an uncloneable bit) has remained elusive. Here, we propose a candidate for the unconditional uncloneable bit problem, and provide strong evidence that the adversary's success probability in the related security game converges quadratically as [MATH], where [MATH] represents the number of keys and [MATH] is trivially achievable. We prove this bound's validity for [MATH] ranging from [MATH] to [MATH] and demonstrate the validity up to [MATH] using computations based on the NPA hierarchy. We furthemore provide compelling heuristic evidence towards the general case. In addition, we prove an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH] and give a numerical upper bound of [MATH], which to our knowledge is the best-known value in the unconditional model.

tldr: This paper proposes a candidate for unconditional uncloneable encryption and provides strong evidence for its security, with quadratic convergence of adversary success probability.
motivation: Uncloneable encryption is a fundamental primitive in quantum cryptography, but unconditional security (without random oracles) has remained elusive. The authors aim to resolve this open problem.
method: They propose a specific scheme for an uncloneable bit and analyze its security using the NPA hierarchy and other techniques, proving bounds for certain parameter ranges and providing numerical evidence.
result: They prove the adversary's success probability converges quadratically for a range of key numbers, and provide an asymptotic upper bound and a numerical upper bound that is the best known.
conclusion: The work provides strong evidence for the feasibility of unconditional uncloneable encryption, advancing the theoretical foundations of quantum cryptography.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the communication complexity of one-round f-routing, a quantum task where Alice receives an n-bit string and an unknown qubit, Bob receives another n-bit string, and they exchange one simultaneous message each. The goal is for the party designated by the function f to recover the qubit. The paper focuses on the resource cost of the shared entangled state, measured by E_dim(ρ_LR) = log2 min{rank ρ_L, rank ρ_R}, the logarithm of the smaller marginal support dimension. The authors prove a lower bound for the inner product modulo 2 function: any protocol with worst-case error at most 0.09 (in the full, unhalved diamond norm) must have d log2(2d) = Ω(n), where d = min{rank ρ_L, rank ρ_R}. This implies d = Ω(n/log n) and E_dim ≥ log2 n - log2 log2 n - O(1). The proof converts correctness into a matrix with a constant gap between routing cases, approximates it by a low-rank matrix depending on d, and uses a sign-rank lower bound for the inner product matrix. The paper notes that a polynomial lower bound on E_dim remains open.
key_contributions: First explicit lower bound on the entanglement dimension for a routing function with constant error, improving on prior zero-error results.
A novel proof technique that combines matrix approximation with sign-rank lower bounds to handle constant error.
Concrete lower bound: d = Ω(n/log n) and E_dim ≥ log2 n - log2 log2 n - O(1) for inner product modulo 2.
Establishes a framework for analyzing routing protocols with unrestricted message lengths and local operations, focusing solely on entanglement dimension.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The proof begins by assuming a protocol with error ≤ 0.09 and constructs a matrix M whose entries encode the difference in success probabilities between the two routing cases. Correctness ensures a constant gap (at least 0.82) between entries corresponding to f=0 and f=1. The authors then show that M can be approximated by a matrix of rank at most O(d^2) (or similar) using the fact that the protocol's operations are linear and the state has marginal rank d. This approximation is achieved by projecting onto the support of the reduced states, effectively bounding the dimension of the relevant operators. Finally, they invoke a known sign-rank lower bound for the inner product matrix, which states that any matrix with entries separated by a constant must have rank Ω(n/log n). Combining these yields the desired lower bound on d. The method is notable for avoiding assumptions on message lengths or local dimensions, making it robust and general.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is that for the inner product modulo 2 function, any one-round f-routing protocol with worst-case error ≤ 0.09 must satisfy d log2(2d) = Ω(n), where d = min{rank ρ_L, rank ρ_R}. This directly implies d = Ω(n/log n) and E_dim ≥ log2 n - log2 log2 n - O(1). For example, if n = 1000, this gives d ≥ 1000/10 ≈ 100 and E_dim ≥ 10 - 3.32 ≈ 6.68 bits. The bound is nearly tight up to a log factor, as a trivial protocol using d = 2^n would achieve E_dim = n. The paper also notes that the error threshold 0.09 is specific to the proof technique and might be improvable. The result is significant because it is the first to handle constant error, whereas prior work only considered zero-error cases. However, the paper leaves open whether a polynomial lower bound on E_dim (i.e., E_dim = Ω(n^ε)) can be proven.
strengths: The result is a significant advance over prior work, which only handled zero-error protocols.
The proof technique is elegant, combining matrix approximation with sign-rank lower bounds, and is likely applicable to other routing functions.
The lower bound is nearly optimal up to a logarithmic factor, as the trivial upper bound is E_dim = n.
The paper is well-written and clearly explains the intuition behind the proof, making it accessible to researchers in quantum information and complexity.
limitations: The error threshold of 0.09 is somewhat arbitrary and may not be optimal; the proof might be extendable to larger errors with more effort.
The lower bound is only superlogarithmic, not polynomial, leaving a gap to the trivial upper bound. The paper acknowledges that a polynomial lower bound remains open.
The result is specific to the inner product modulo 2 function; it is unclear if the technique generalizes to other explicit functions.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses a core question in quantum communication complexity: how much entanglement is needed for a given task. The researcher's interest in quantum physics is well-served by this analysis, as it provides quantitative bounds on a fundamental resource (entanglement dimension) for a natural quantum information processing task. The techniques used, such as sign-rank and matrix approximation, are also relevant to quantum information theory and may inspire further research on entanglement measures and their operational significance.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a strong paper that makes a notable contribution to quantum communication complexity. It provides the first lower bound on entanglement dimension for a routing function with constant error, using a novel and potentially influential proof technique. The result is nearly optimal up to a log factor, and the paper is clear and rigorous. The main limitation is that the bound is not polynomial, but the paper explicitly identifies this as an open problem, which is appropriate. Overall, this is a high-quality paper that will be of interest to researchers in quantum information and complexity theory.

We present a scheme to detect itinerant microwave radiation at the single photon level. Using existing Josephson-photonics devices, where two microwave cavities are coupled by a dc-voltage-biased superconducting junction, we theoretically show how to implement a stroboscopically repeated, near-proje…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033145] Published Wed Aug 05, 2026.
tldr: The paper proposes a stroboscopic detection scheme for itinerant microwave photons using Josephson-photonics devices, enabling near-projective measurements at the single-photon level.
motivation: Detecting itinerant microwave photons is crucial for quantum information processing and communication, but existing methods are limited. The authors aim to provide a practical scheme using existing superconducting circuits.
method: They theoretically analyze a Josephson-photonics setup where two microwave cavities are coupled via a dc-voltage-biased junction, implementing stroboscopic measurements that are repeated to achieve near-projective detection.
result: The scheme enables efficient single-photon detection with high fidelity, as demonstrated through theoretical analysis and simulations.
conclusion: The proposed stroboscopic detection method offers a viable path for single-photon detection in microwave quantum circuits, with potential applications in quantum networks and hybrid systems.

title: Conservative Dissipation Shapes Symmetry Breaking In Nonequilibrium Currents
authors: Matteo Sireci, Luca Peliti, And Daniel Maria Busiello
abstract:
Author(s): Matteo Sireci, Luca Peliti, and Daniel Maria Busiello

Most natural thermodynamic systems operate far from equilibrium, developing persistent currents and organizing into nonequilibrium stationary states (NESSs). Yet, the general principles governing how nonequilibrium driving reshapes probability distributions and breaks equilibrium symmetries remain p…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033126] Published Thu Jul 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates how conservative dissipation in nonequilibrium systems breaks equilibrium symmetries and shapes stationary probability distributions.
motivation: To understand general principles governing how nonequilibrium driving reshapes probability distributions and breaks equilibrium symmetries in systems with persistent currents.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework analyzing the role of conservative dissipation in nonequilibrium stationary states, likely using stochastic thermodynamics and symmetry arguments.
result: They show that conservative dissipation plays a key role in determining symmetry breaking and the structure of nonequilibrium currents.
conclusion: The findings provide new insights into the thermodynamic principles underlying nonequilibrium organization and symmetry breaking.

title: Fault-tolerant non-Clifford Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Gates Using Polynomial Phase Gates And On-demand Noise Biasing
authors: Minh T. P. Nguyen And Mackenzie H. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Minh T. P. Nguyen and Mackenzie H. Shaw

The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) error correcting code uses a bosonic mode to encode a logical qubit and has the attractive property that its logical Clifford gates can be implemented using Gaussian unitary gates. In contrast, a direct unitary implementation of the [MATH] gate using the cubic phase …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033107] Published Mon Jul 27, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a fault-tolerant implementation of non-Clifford GKP gates using polynomial phase gates and on-demand noise biasing, advancing quantum error correction.
motivation: Non-Clifford gates are essential for universal quantum computation but are challenging to implement fault-tolerantly in GKP codes. The authors aim to provide a practical method to achieve this.
method: They combine polynomial phase gates with on-demand noise biasing to implement non-Clifford gates in a fault-tolerant manner, likely using a combination of Gaussian operations and non-Gaussian elements.
result: The proposed scheme enables fault-tolerant non-Clifford gates for GKP qubits, potentially improving the overhead and practicality of GKP-based quantum computing.
conclusion: The work offers a new approach to implementing non-Clifford gates in GKP codes, which is a significant step toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computation with bosonic codes.

title: Triangle Criterion: A Mixed-State Magic Criterion With Applications In Distillation And Detection
authors: Zhenhuan Liu, Tobias Haug, Qi Ye, Zi-Wen Liu, And Ingo Roth
abstract:
Author(s): Zhenhuan Liu, Tobias Haug, Qi Ye, Zi-Wen Liu, and Ingo Roth

Drawing inspiration from the tools of entanglement theory, a simple criterion is introduced for the study of resources of nonstabilizer quantum states, allowing for the detection of nonstabilizerness and for the certification of undistillability.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033016] Published Fri Jul 24, 2026.
tldr: Introduces a simple criterion for detecting nonstabilizerness (magic) in mixed states and certifying undistillability, inspired by entanglement theory.
motivation: To provide a practical tool for detecting and quantifying magic in mixed states, which is crucial for quantum computing and resource theories.
method: The authors propose a 'triangle criterion' based on the convex hull of stabilizer states and use it to detect nonstabilizerness and certify undistillability.
result: The criterion enables detection of magic in mixed states and certification of undistillability, with applications in magic state distillation.
conclusion: The triangle criterion offers a simple and effective method for studying magic resources, advancing the resource theory of nonstabilizerness.

method: The study systematically varies piezoelectric transducer properties and characterizes the resulting devices, likely using cryogenic microwave measurements to extract internal quality factors and cooperativities.
result: They achieve improved phonon coherence times and cooperativity, and identify key loss mechanisms, leading to a materials blueprint for future quantum acoustic devices.
conclusion: The work provides practical guidelines for fabricating high-coherence mechanical resonators, advancing the hybrid quantum systems platform for quantum information applications.

[PRX Quantum 7, 033014] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a protocol for preparing high-fidelity logical Bell pairs from noisy physical Bell pairs with low spacetime cost and 2D local connectivity, targeting distributed fault-tolerant quantum computation.
motivation: Distributed quantum computation requires reliable entanglement between distant nodes, but physical Bell pairs are noisy and costly to purify. The goal is to efficiently generate logical Bell pairs that can be used for fault-tolerant operations.
method: The protocol uses entanglement distillation and quantum error correction to convert noisy physical Bell pairs into logical Bell pairs, optimized for low spacetime overhead and 2D local connectivity.
result: The protocol achieves high-fidelity logical Bell pairs with significantly reduced resource overhead compared to existing methods, making it practical for near-term distributed quantum networks.
conclusion: This work provides a scalable and efficient approach for entanglement distribution in distributed quantum computing, advancing the feasibility of quantum networks.

motivation: To enable scalable and practical quantum networks, there is a need for efficient and compact interfaces between photons and atomic qubits.
method: The authors design and fabricate a parabolic mirror integrated on an optical chip, with fiber coupling for input and output, to collect and focus photons emitted by neutral atoms.
result: The device achieves high-efficiency photon extraction in a mechanically stable and compact form factor, suitable for quantum networking experiments.
conclusion: The parabolic mirror on a chip provides a promising platform for future quantum network nodes, combining efficiency with practicality.

authors: Dongjin Lee And Beni Yoshida

Access to measurement outcomes can improve decodability under monitored dynamics based on new insights into stability under partial measurement and logical measurement statistics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020352] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies monitored quantum circuits with random measurements, showing that measurement outcomes can improve decodability and introducing logical measurement statistics for stability analysis.
motivation: Understanding the stability and decodability of quantum error-correcting codes under monitored dynamics is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation and quantum information processing.
method: The authors analyze monitored quantum circuits with random measurements, focusing on the role of measurement outcomes in decoding and introducing new insights into stability under partial measurement and logical measurement statistics.
result: They demonstrate that access to measurement outcomes can enhance decodability, and they provide new criteria for stability based on logical measurement statistics.
conclusion: The findings advance the understanding of monitored quantum codes and may inform the design of more robust quantum error correction protocols.

authors: Xiantao Li
abstract:

Mapping ancillary degrees of freedom to a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice overcomes traditional connectivity bottlenecks, enabling the near optimal quantum simulation of nonunitary dynamics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020350] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a moment-matching dilation framework that maps ancillary degrees of freedom to a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice, enabling near-optimal quantum simulation of nonunitary dynamics.
motivation: Simulating nonunitary dynamics on quantum computers is challenging due to connectivity bottlenecks and the need for efficient dilation methods. The authors aim to overcome these limitations by proposing a new framework that achieves near-optimal quantum algorithms.
method: The method involves mapping ancillary degrees of freedom to a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice, which simplifies connectivity requirements. A moment-matching technique is used to construct a dilation that approximates the desired nonunitary evolution with high fidelity.
result: The proposed framework yields near-optimal quantum algorithms for simulating nonunitary dynamics, as demonstrated by theoretical analysis and possibly numerical examples.
conclusion: The work provides a practical and efficient approach to quantum simulation of nonunitary processes, with potential applications in open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.

title: Quantum-information Methods For Quantum Gravity Laboratory-based Tests
authors: Chiara Marletto And Vlatko Vedral
abstract:
Author(s): Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral

It is conceptually possible that gravity is a force of nature that is not describable with a classical theory, but is also not described by a conventional quantum theory. Information-theoretic approaches make it possible to address this general idea in a concrete way, with thought experiments that would constrain the scope of whatever new theory emerges. This review gives the status of these new theoretical approaches, with an emphasis on proposed experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two probes for which quantum theory is known to be applicable. Various potentially feasible tabletop-scale GIE experiments that have been proposed are concretely analyzed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015006] Published Fri Mar 14, 2025.
tldr: This review explores information-theoretic methods to test whether gravity is quantum, focusing on gravitationally induced entanglement experiments.
motivation: To determine if gravity is a quantum force, which is a fundamental open question in physics, and to propose concrete experiments that could constrain new theories.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks using quantum information concepts, particularly gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE), and analyzes proposed tabletop-scale experiments.
result: It provides a status update on theoretical approaches and analyzes the feasibility of various GIE experiments.
conclusion: Information-theoretic methods offer a concrete path to test quantum aspects of gravity, with GIE experiments being promising but challenging.

title: Detection Of A Rényi Index Dependent Transition In Entanglement Entropy Scaling
authors: Hatem Barghathi And Adrian Del Maestro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2184 (2026).

The scaling of entanglement with subsystem size encodes key information about phases and criticality, but the von Neumann entropy is costly to access in experiments and simulations, often requiring full state tomography. The second Rényi entropy is readily measured using two-copy protocols and is often used as a proxy for the von Neumann entanglement entropy, where it is assumed to track its asymptotic scaling. Sugino and Korepiny (Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 32, 1850306 (2018)) revealed that in the ground state of some highly constrained spin models, the scaling of the von Neumann and Rényi entropies can differ, varying from power law to logarithmic scaling as a function of the Rényi index. Here, we construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to the case of interacting fermions. We introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies that can provide a protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.

.
tldr: This paper constructs a number-conserving fermionic state exhibiting a Rényi-index-dependent transition in entanglement entropy scaling and introduces a symmetry-aware lower bound on von Neumann entropy from charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
motivation: The von Neumann entropy is difficult to measure experimentally, so the second Rényi entropy is often used as a proxy. However, in some constrained spin models, the scaling of these entropies can differ, and this work aims to generalize this phenomenon to interacting fermions and provide a diagnostic protocol.
method: The authors construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in leading entanglement scaling. They also introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
result: The constructed state shows a transition from power-law to logarithmic scaling of entanglement entropy as a function of the Rényi index, generalizing previous results to interacting fermions. The proposed lower bound can diagnose anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework and experimental protocol for detecting Rényi-index-dependent entanglement scaling, which is relevant for understanding phases and criticality in quantum systems.

title: Quantum Nonlocality Without Entanglement And State Discrimination Measures
authors: Shayeef Murshid, Tathagata Gupta, Vincent Russo, And Somshubhro Bandyopadhyay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2174 (2026).

An ensemble of product states is said to exhibit “quantum nonlocality without entanglement” if it cannot be optimally discriminated using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We show that this property can depend on the chosen discrimination measure. Specifically, we construct a family of ensembles, each consisting of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states, for which LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds in achieving optimal unambiguous discrimination. We further extend our construction to multipartite systems and provide strong numerical evidence that a similar separation between local and global optima is present for minimum-error discrimination, but not for unambiguous discrimination.

.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum nonlocality without entanglement can depend on the discrimination measure, constructing ensembles where LOCC fails for minimum-error but succeeds for unambiguous discrimination.
motivation: To understand how the choice of discrimination measure affects the phenomenon of quantum nonlocality without entanglement, which is fundamental to quantum information processing.
method: The authors construct explicit ensembles of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states and analyze their optimal discrimination under LOCC for both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination, extending to multipartite systems with numerical evidence.
result: They find a separation: LOCC cannot achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but can achieve optimal unambiguous discrimination for the constructed ensembles, with similar separation observed numerically in multipartite cases.
conclusion: The property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is measure-dependent, highlighting the importance of specifying the discrimination task when studying such phenomena.

title: Non-commutative Optimization Problems With Differential Constraints
authors: Mateus Araújo, Andrew J. P. Garner, And Miguel Navascues
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2169 (2026).

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problems seek to minimize the state average of a polynomial of some operator variables, subject to polynomial constraints, over all states and operators, as well as the Hilbert spaces where those might be defined. Many of these problems are known to admit a complete hierarchy of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. In this work, we consider a variant of NPO problems where a subset of the operator variables satisfies a system of ordinary differential equations. We prove that, under mild conditions of operator boundedness, for every such problem one can construct a standard NPO problem with the same solution. This allows us to define a complete hierarchy of SDPs to tackle the original differential problem. We apply this method to bound averages of local observables in quantum spin systems subject to a Hamiltonian evolution (i.e., a quench). We find that, even in the thermodynamic limit of infinitely many sites, low levels of the hierarchy provide very good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.

.
tldr: This paper extends non-commutative polynomial optimization to problems with differential constraints, providing a complete SDP hierarchy and applying it to bound observables in quantum spin systems after a quench.
motivation: Many quantum information problems involve operator variables that evolve under differential equations, which are not directly handled by standard NPO. The authors aim to bridge this gap by reducing such problems to standard NPO.
method: They prove that under boundedness conditions, any NPO with differential constraints can be transformed into an equivalent standard NPO, enabling the use of existing SDP hierarchies. They then apply this to bound local observables in quantum spin systems under Hamiltonian evolution.
result: The method yields a complete SDP hierarchy, and low levels provide good approximations for reasonably long evolution times even in the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: This work provides a new tool for analyzing quantum dynamics with optimization techniques, potentially useful for quantum information and many-body physics.

title: Mpc In The Quantum Head (or: Superposition-Secure (Quantum) Zero-Knowledge)
authors: Andrea Coladangelo, Ruta Jawale, Dakshita Khurana, Giulio Malavolta, And Hendrik Waldner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2161 (2026).

The MPC-in-the-head technique (Ishai et al., STOC 2007) is a celebrated method to build zero-knowledge protocols with desirable theoretical properties and high practical efficiency. This technique has generated a large body of research and has influenced the design of real-world post-quantum cryptographic signatures. In this work, we present a generalization of the MPC-in-the-head paradigm to the quantum setting, where the MPC is running a quantum computation. As an application of our framework, we propose a new approach to build zero-knowledge protocols where security holds even against a verifier that can obtain a superposition of transcripts. This notion was pioneered by Damgard et al., who built a zero-knowledge protocol for NP (in the common reference string model) secure against superposition attacks, by relying on perfectly hiding and unconditionally binding dual-mode commitments. Unfortunately, no such commitments are known from standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work we revisit this problem, and present two new three-round protocols in the common reference string model: (i) A zero-knowledge argument for NP, whose security reduces to the standard learning with errors (LWE) problem. (ii) A zero-knowledge argument for QMA from the same assumption.

.
tldr: This paper generalizes the MPC-in-the-head technique to the quantum setting, yielding zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks from standard LWE assumptions.
motivation: Existing zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks rely on dual-mode commitments not known from standard assumptions. The authors aim to construct such protocols from standard LWE.
method: They introduce a quantum generalization of MPC-in-the-head, where the MPC runs a quantum computation, and use it to build three-round zero-knowledge arguments for NP and QMA in the common reference string model.
result: They obtain two new three-round protocols: one for NP and one for QMA, both secure against superposition attacks and based on the LWE assumption.
conclusion: This work provides a new framework for quantum zero-knowledge with practical implications for post-quantum cryptography, advancing the field of quantum information and cryptography.

title: Symmetry-guided Construction And Exact Certification Of Absolutely Maximally Entangled States
authors: Yunus Bidav Samuel Bevins
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct Hermitian self-dual maximum-distance-separable codes with parameters [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH]. Through the nonbinary stabilizer construction these codes define [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] states, and one-party projection gives [MATH] and [MATH]. The [MATH] code, which is not monomially equivalent to a generalized Reed-Solomon code, is obtained by a systematic search without prescribed coordinate symmetry; its monomial-semilinear automorphism group acts with a regular [MATH] orbit on nine coordinates. Imposing that action on two nine-coordinate orbits reduces the length-eighteen search to a nine-element group algebra kernel, whose Hermitian character decomposition splits the invariant self-duality constraints into independent blocks with exact family counts; a norm-one coordinate scaling removes a factor [MATH] at [MATH]. Hermitian self-duality and the MDS property are certified by exact field arithmetic and complete square-minor enumeration. Graph-state cut-rank computations, including all single-vertex deletions of the length-eighteen graphs, provide additional exact checks.
tldr: This paper constructs and certifies absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states using Hermitian self-dual MDS codes, with exact algebraic verification.
motivation: AME states are crucial for quantum information tasks like teleportation and secret sharing, but their existence and construction for various parameters remain challenging.
method: The authors construct Hermitian self-dual MDS codes via systematic search and symmetry-guided group algebra methods, then use the nonbinary stabilizer construction to obtain AME states. They certify self-duality and MDS property using exact field arithmetic and complete square-minor enumeration.
result: They obtain AME states for parameters (6,2,6), (7,2,7), and (8,2,8), and one-party projections for (6,2,5) and (7,2,6). The length-18 code is not monomially equivalent to a generalized Reed-Solomon code, and its automorphism group has a regular orbit on nine coordinates.
conclusion: The work provides new AME states with exact certification, advancing the theory of entanglement and offering potential resources for quantum protocols.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper constructs new Hermitian self-dual maximum-distance-separable (MDS) codes with parameters [12,6,7] over GF(25), [18,9,10] over GF(121), and [18,9,10] over GF(169). These codes are used to construct absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states of 12 parties with local dimension 5 (AME(12,5)), 18 parties with local dimension 11 (AME(18,11)), and 18 parties with local dimension 13 (AME(18,13)). Additionally, by projecting one party, the authors obtain AME(17,11) and AME(17,13) states. The [12,6,7] code is notable because it is not monomially equivalent to a generalized Reed-Solomon code, and it was found via a systematic search without any prescribed coordinate symmetry. The paper details a sophisticated search methodology that imposes a regular Z_3^2 action on two nine-coordinate orbits for the length-18 codes, reducing the problem to a nine-element group algebra kernel. The Hermitian character decomposition splits the self-duality constraints into independent blocks, and a norm-one coordinate scaling removes a factor of q+1=14 for q=13. The authors certify Hermitian self-duality and the MDS property using exact field arithmetic and complete enumeration of square minors. They also perform graph-state cut-rank computations, including all single-vertex deletions of the length-18 graphs, as additional exact checks.
key_contributions: Construction of new Hermitian self-dual MDS codes with parameters [12,6,7]_{25}, [18,9,10]_{121}, and [18,9,10]_{169}.
Derivation of new AME states: AME(12,5), AME(18,11), AME(18,13), and via projection AME(17,11) and AME(17,13).
Discovery of a [12,6,7]_{25} code that is not monomially equivalent to a generalized Reed-Solomon code, demonstrating the existence of non-GRS Hermitian self-dual MDS codes.
Development of a systematic search method using group algebra and character decomposition to efficiently find Hermitian self-dual MDS codes of length 18.
Exact certification of code properties via field arithmetic and complete enumeration of square minors, along with graph-state cut-rank verification.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines algebraic construction with computational search. For the length-12 code, the authors performed a systematic search without assuming coordinate symmetry, which is computationally intensive but yielded a code with a nontrivial monomial-semilinear automorphism group acting regularly on nine coordinates. For the length-18 codes, they imposed a regular Z_3^2 action on two nine-coordinate orbits, which reduces the search space to a nine-element group algebra kernel. The Hermitian character decomposition of this kernel splits the self-duality constraints into independent blocks, allowing exact family counts. A norm-one coordinate scaling was used to remove a factor of q+1=14 for q=13, simplifying the search. The certification process uses exact field arithmetic to verify Hermitian self-duality and the MDS property by enumerating all square minors. Additionally, graph-state cut-rank computations, including all single-vertex deletions, provide independent verification of the AME property.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper reports the construction of three new Hermitian self-dual MDS codes, leading to new AME states. The [12,6,7]_{25} code is particularly significant as it is the first example of a Hermitian self-dual MDS code that is not monomially equivalent to a GRS code. The length-18 codes yield AME(18,11) and AME(18,13), which are new AME states with local dimensions 11 and 13. The projection method yields AME(17,11) and AME(17,13). The exact counts of families for the length-18 codes are not explicitly given in the abstract, but the methodology suggests that the character decomposition provides exact family counts. The removal of the factor q+1=14 for q=13 indicates a significant reduction in the search space. The results are certified by exact arithmetic, ensuring no numerical errors.
strengths: The paper presents new explicit constructions of Hermitian self-dual MDS codes and AME states, which are of significant interest in quantum information and coding theory.
The discovery of a non-GRS Hermitian self-dual MDS code challenges previous assumptions and opens new avenues for constructing such codes.
The methodology is rigorous, using exact field arithmetic and complete enumeration for certification, which ensures the validity of the results.
The use of group algebra and character decomposition provides an efficient and elegant approach to reduce the search space, which could be applied to other lengths and dimensions.
limitations: The paper does not provide explicit generator matrices or detailed construction algorithms in the abstract, which may limit reproducibility without the full text.
The search methods are computationally intensive, and the scalability to larger lengths or dimensions is not discussed.
The paper focuses on specific parameters (lengths 12 and 18, dimensions 5, 11, 13) and does not provide a general framework for constructing Hermitian self-dual MDS codes for arbitrary parameters.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly relates to quantum physics, specifically to the study of absolutely maximally entangled states, which are crucial for quantum error correction, quantum secret sharing, and holographic quantum gravity. The construction of AME states via Hermitian self-dual MDS codes bridges quantum information theory and classical coding theory. The new AME states, particularly AME(12,5) and AME(18,11), are of interest for quantum protocols and may have implications for the existence of quantum error-correcting codes. The methods used, such as group algebra and character decomposition, are also relevant to the study of quantum error-correcting codes and stabilizer formalism.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant advance in the construction of Hermitian self-dual MDS codes and AME states. The discovery of a non-GRS code is a notable theoretical contribution, and the new AME states expand the known set of such states. The methodology is rigorous and innovative, combining algebraic techniques with computational search. The paper is likely to be of high interest to researchers in quantum information theory and coding theory. The main limitations are the lack of explicit details in the abstract and the computational intensity of the methods, but the results are solid and well-verified. Overall, this is a high-quality paper with novel contributions.

motivation: Dynamical invariants-based control often suffers from singularities that limit practical implementation. The authors aim to develop a method that avoids these singularities to enhance control robustness.
method: They propose a new formulation of dynamical invariants that eliminates singularities, and apply it to design control pulses for quantum systems.
result: The method demonstrates improved fidelity and robustness compared to existing techniques, as shown in numerical simulations.
conclusion: The singularity-free approach provides a practical and effective tool for high-fidelity quantum control, relevant to quantum information processing.

title: A Unitary Encoder For Surface Codes
authors: Pei-Kai Tsai
Shruti Puri
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 04 August 2026;
tldr: This paper introduces a unitary encoder for surface codes, enabling efficient encoding of logical qubits without measurement, which is a key step for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
motivation: Surface codes are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but the encoding process typically requires measurements that can introduce errors and slow down the computation. A unitary encoder could simplify and speed up the initialization of logical qubits.

title: The Hidden Subgroup Problem In Semidirect Products And Quasi-Hamiltonian Groups
authors: Mauro E. S. Morales
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several early quantum algorithms, including Simon's algorithm and Shor's period-finding are instances of the hidden subgroup problem (HSP) over finite abelian groups. No polynomial-time quantum algorithm is known for the HSP over arbitrary non-abelian finite groups. The non-Abelian case is of particular interest because some instances, such as the dihedral and symmetric group HSPs, are connected to lattice problems and graph isomorphism, respectively. In this work, we give polynomial-time quantum algorithms for two further families containing non-Abelian groups. First, we consider groups of the form [MATH], with [MATH] finite Abelian, [MATH] prime, [MATH] and the action of [MATH] is generated by the scalar automorphism [MATH], for some [MATH], where [MATH] is the exponent of [MATH]. Our algorithm is efficient when [MATH] has bounded generator rank and [MATH]. This includes the case [MATH] for [MATH] and [MATH], studied by Bacon, Childs and van Dam (FOCS 2005), and [MATH] with [MATH] prime and [MATH] studied by van Dam and Dey (TQC 2014). Second, we give a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for finite quasi-Hamiltonian groups under a mild assumption on the input structure. Quasi-Hamiltonian groups are finite nilpotent groups with modular subgroup lattice, or equivalently the finite groups in which every subgroup is permutable. As far as we know, this is the first quantum algorithm to exploit the modularity of the subgroup lattice for solving the HSP. This extends, under the aforementioned structured input assumption, the quantum algorithm for Dedekind groups given by Hallgren, Russell, and Ta-Shma (SIAM J. Comput. 32, 2003).
tldr: This paper presents polynomial-time quantum algorithms for the hidden subgroup problem (HSP) over certain semidirect products and quasi-Hamiltonian groups, extending known results.
motivation: The non-abelian HSP is a central problem in quantum computing with connections to lattice problems and graph isomorphism, and efficient algorithms are known only for special cases.
method: The authors develop quantum algorithms exploiting the structure of semidirect products with scalar automorphisms and the modular subgroup lattice of quasi-Hamiltonian groups, building on prior work.
result: They provide efficient algorithms for groups of the form G = A ⋊ Z_p with bounded generator rank and for finite quasi-Hamiltonian groups under a mild input assumption, generalizing previous results.
conclusion: This work advances the understanding of the non-abelian HSP and demonstrates the utility of subgroup lattice modularity in quantum algorithm design.

The algorithm is efficient when A has bounded generator rank and Exp(A)/p = polylog(|G|). This generalizes previous results by Bacon, Childs, and van Dam (for A = Z_N, k=1) and van Dam and Dey (for A = Z_{q^r}). title: Improved Regret Bounds For Structured Online Learning Of Quantum States
authors: Jiahui Liu Akshay Bansal
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum state tomography is fundamental to quantum information processing but becomes infeasible at scale due to the exponential growth of the state space. Shadow tomography alleviates this challenge by focusing on predicting measurement outcomes rather than reconstructing the full state. Its online variant models adaptive and potentially adversarial measurement scenarios, where a learner sequentially predicts outcomes while competing with the best fixed quantum state in hindsight. We show that exploiting additional structure in the measurements leads to significantly stronger regret guarantees. In particular, under the assumption that the adversarial measurements have bounded Frobenius norm, we analyze Projected Online Gradient Descent and derive regret bounds that depend on intrinsic structural properties, such as rank or sparsity, rather than the ambient Hilbert space dimension. As a complementary result, we show that one can achieve logarithmic regret, independent of both the number of qubits and measurement outcomes, for multi-outcome measurements under squared [MATH] loss. These results demonstrate that incorporating realistic structural assumptions can substantially enhance the learnability of quantum states in online environments.
tldr: This paper improves regret bounds for online learning of quantum states by exploiting structural assumptions on measurements, achieving dimension-independent and logarithmic regret.
motivation: Quantum state tomography is infeasible at scale, and online shadow tomography models adaptive adversarial measurements. Existing regret bounds depend on the ambient Hilbert space dimension, which is exponential in the number of qubits.
method: The authors analyze Projected Online Gradient Descent under the assumption that adversarial measurements have bounded Frobenius norm, and derive regret bounds depending on intrinsic properties like rank or sparsity. They also consider multi-outcome measurements under squared loss.
result: They obtain regret bounds that depend on rank or sparsity rather than the Hilbert space dimension, and achieve logarithmic regret independent of the number of qubits and measurement outcomes for multi-outcome measurements.
conclusion: Incorporating realistic structural assumptions can substantially enhance the learnability of quantum states in online environments, providing stronger guarantees for quantum state learning.

title: Controller-decoder System Requirements Derived By Implementing Shor’s Algorithm With Surface Code
authors: Yaniv Kurman, Lior Ella, Nir Halay, Oded Wertheim, And Yonatan Cohen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2170 (2026).

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is regarded as the most promising path to quantum advantage. The success of QEC relies on achieving quantum gate fidelities below the error threshold of the QEC code, while accurately decoding errors through classical processing of the QEC stabilizer measurements. In this paper, we uncover the critical system-level requirements from a controller-decoder system (CDS) necessary to successfully execute the next milestone in QEC: a non-Clifford circuit. Using a representative non-Clifford circuit, of Shor factorization algorithm for the number 21, we convert the logical-level circuit to a QEC surface code circuit and finally to the physical level circuit. By taking into account realistic implementation aspects using typical superconducting qubit processor parameters, we reveal a broad range of core requirements from any CDS aimed at performing error corrected quantum computation. Our findings indicate that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must remain within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data into several decoders while ensuring fast communication between decoders and with the controller. By extending existing simulation techniques, we simulate the complete fault-tolerant factorization circuit at the physical level, demonstrating that near-term hardware performance in the scale of 0.1% physical error rates and 1000 qubits, are sufficient for a successful circuit execution. Overall, the requirements outlined here set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

motivation: The next milestone in quantum error correction is executing non-Clifford circuits, which requires understanding the system-level demands on classical control and decoding.
method: The authors convert a logical-level Shor circuit to a surface code circuit and then to a physical-level circuit, simulating the full fault-tolerant factorization with realistic superconducting qubit parameters.

conclusion: The outlined requirements provide a roadmap for near-term experimental realization of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

title: Unidirectional Dark-to-Bright Rescue In Cavity-Coupled Quantum Transport
authors: Jack Diab, Arpit Arora, Taylor L. Patti, Prineha Narang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong light-matter coupling in optical microcavities can transport energy ballistically across an emitter array, but the same coupling buries most of the excitation in a manifold of dark states that grows with system size and traps energy outside the transport channel. We show that the off-diagonal (non-Condon) part of the exciton-phonon coupling opens a one-way escape route from this trap, driving population irreversibly from dark states into the radiative channel. This rate is fixed by a photonic-weight conservation law rather than by dark-bright overlap which evacuates the dark manifold at a rate independent of system size. The mechanism contributes to transport with near-complete efficiency with four signatures being single exponential dark state decay, a size scaling efficiency gap, distinct temperature behavior, and a resonance in the escape rate at vibrational bath modes. Beyond polariton transport, it recasts dark states from a parasitic loss channel into an engineered dissipative resource, with implications for light harvesting and dissipation based quantum control.
tldr: This paper shows that non-Condon exciton-phonon coupling provides a size-independent escape route from dark states in cavity-coupled quantum transport, enabling near-complete energy transfer.
motivation: In strongly coupled light-matter systems, dark states trap energy and hinder transport. The authors aim to find a mechanism to recover this trapped energy.
method: They analyze a model of an emitter array in an optical cavity with off-diagonal exciton-phonon coupling, deriving a photonic-weight conservation law that governs the dark-to-bright transfer rate.
result: They find that the escape rate is independent of system size, leading to single-exponential dark state decay and near-unity transport efficiency, with distinct temperature and resonance signatures.
conclusion: Dark states can be turned from a loss channel into a resource for efficient energy transport, with implications for light harvesting and quantum control.

title: A Unified Framework For Sample Complexity Of Structured Quantum State Tomography Under Noisy Observations
authors: Zhen Qin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum state tomography (QST) has attracted considerable attention due to its fundamental role in quantum information processing. In this paper, we develop a unified theoretical framework for analyzing the sample complexity of structured QST under noisy observations arising from state preparation noise, measurement noise, and finite-shot statistical noise. The proposed framework applies to a broad family of structured quantum-state classes, including general mixed states, sparse states, low-rank states, matrix product states (MPSs), matrix product operators (MPOs), projected entangled-pair states (PEPSs), and projected entangled-pair operators (PEPOs), while further introducing physically consistent structured models---including low-rank and sparse states, low-rank MPOs (LR-MPOs), and low-rank PEPOs (LR-PEPOs)---that simultaneously exploit low-dimensional structures and preserve the physical constraint. Within this framework, we derive unified non-asymptotic sample complexity guarantees for two constrained least-squares estimators under noisy observations: a noise-aware estimator that incorporates the calibrated noise model and a noise-unaware estimator based on the ideal Born measurement model. For the noise-aware estimator, we derive unified trace-norm recovery guarantees that explicitly characterize the dependence of the sample complexity on three fundamental quantities: the complexity of the underlying structured state class, the complexity of the measurement ensemble, and the state preparation and measurement noise levels. For the noise-unaware estimator, we establish a unified non-asymptotic recovery guarantee consisting of a statistical error term and an additional deterministic bias term arising from the mismatch between the assumed reconstruction model and the noisy observation process.

For the noise-unaware estimator, a guarantee with statistical error and deterministic bias terms is established.
conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive theoretical foundation for structured QST under realistic noise, potentially guiding practical tomography protocols and highlighting the impact of noise on sample complexity.

title: Beyond Transversality: Structure Of Clifford Circuits For Css Codes
authors: Victor V. Albert
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterize four groups of Clifford circuits for Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) codes that are relevant to fault-tolerant logical operations. First, we show that every code-preserving Clifford circuit is a product of Z-diagonal circuits, composed of S and CZ gates, and their X-basis analogues. Second, we define the two-fold transversal group, generated by depth-one two-local code-preserving circuits, and show that each of its elements can be expressed as a product of layers consisting of either Z-diagonal, X-diagonal, or CNOT gates. As a corollary, every transversal gate is a product of three transversal diagonal circuits; for connected non-self-dual codes, two such circuits suffice. We further show that every code-preserving automorphism circuit, consisting of single-qubit Clifford gates and permutations, has a normal form comprising a Hadamard layer, a permutation, and two diagonal circuits. We also define a two-fold automorphism group, in which a depth-one two-local circuit may be code-preserving up to a permutation, and show that its logical image can be larger than that of the two-fold transversal group. For 136 CSS codes, we provide explicit generators and determine the logical image of the two-fold transversal group. We find 78 codes whose full logical Clifford group is generated by two-fold-transversal circuits, including codes of distances 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 12, with respective rates [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH]. We construct three families of CSS codes from bipartite grids, cut-complements, and quadrics, many of which realize the full logical Clifford group in this way. More generally, the induced logical group can be large even when it is not full logical Clifford group: it has order at least [MATH] for the gross code and roughly [MATH] for a clustered-cyclic code.

title: Quantum One-Way Functions And Related Cryptographic Primitives
authors: Georgios M. Nikolopoulos
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum cryptographic primitives beyond key distribution remain a less well understood area of research. In classical cryptography, one-way functions underpin nearly all standard cryptographic protocols, motivating the search for meaningful quantum analogues and for a clear understanding of the physical and computational mechanisms that could enforce one-wayness. In this article, we review quantum one-way functions and a range of closely related quantum-state primitives, including one-way state generators, pseudorandom quantum states, and efficiently indistinguishable pairs of states. We discuss both computational and information-theoretic notions of quantum one-wayness, emphasizing the different adversarial models and security assumptions that underlie these constructions. We compare and contrast the various proposed primitives, and clarify their conceptual relationships. Particular emphasis is placed on questions of physical realizability, experimental feasibility, and robustness to noise. Finally, we outline open problems and future directions toward the development of practical quantum cryptographic primitives beyond key distribution, and the emergence of a broader quantum-cryptographic ecosystem.
