A novel spectroscopy method leverages single-shot readouts to extract noise cross-correlations, successfully bridging the elusive intermediate-frequency gap in qubit noise characterization.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020351] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a novel spectroscopy method using single-shot readouts to extract noise cross-correlations, bridging the intermediate-frequency gap in qubit noise characterization.
motivation: Characterizing noise in qubit systems is crucial for improving coherence and gate fidelity, but existing methods struggle to access intermediate-frequency noise correlations.
method: The authors propose a spectroscopy technique that leverages single-shot measurements to extract noise cross-correlations, enabling the study of noise in a frequency range previously difficult to access.
result: The method successfully bridges the intermediate-frequency gap, providing a new tool for qubit noise characterization.
conclusion: This approach offers a practical way to measure noise cross-correlations in qubit systems, which could aid in understanding and mitigating decoherence.

title: Collective Enhancement Of Photon Blockade Via Two-Photon Interactions
authors: Lijuan Dong, Aanal Jayesh Shah, Peter Kirton, Hadiseh Alaeian, And Simone Felicetti
abstract:
Author(s): Lijuan Dong, Aanal Jayesh Shah, Peter Kirton, Hadiseh Alaeian, and Simone Felicetti

Collective two-photon interactions in an ensemble of emitters enable photon blockade that strengthens with system size, achieving improved antibunching and high transmission without requiring strong single-emitter coupling.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020349] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that collective two-photon interactions in an ensemble of emitters can enhance photon blockade, improving antibunching and transmission without strong single-emitter coupling.
motivation: Photon blockade typically requires strong single-emitter coupling, which is challenging to achieve. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by exploiting collective effects in an ensemble.
method: They theoretically analyze a system of many emitters coupled to a cavity, focusing on two-photon interactions and deriving conditions for collective photon blockade.
result: They find that photon blockade is collectively enhanced with system size, leading to improved antibunching and high transmission even when single-emitter coupling is weak.
conclusion: Collective two-photon interactions offer a promising route to achieve efficient photon blockade in hybrid quantum systems, potentially benefiting quantum information processing and networking.

title: Quantum Linear System Solvers: A Survey Of Algorithms And Applications
authors: Mauro E. S. Morales, Lirandë Pira, Philipp Schleich, Kelvin Koor, Pedro C. S. Costa, Dong An, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Lin Lin, Patrick Rebentrost, And Dominic W. Berry
abstract:
Author(s): Mauro E. S. Morales, Lirandë Pira, Philipp Schleich, Kelvin Koor, Pedro C. S. Costa, Dong An, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Lin Lin, Patrick Rebentrost, and Dominic W. Berry

Given vector b and matrix
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025005] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive survey of quantum algorithms for solving linear systems, from HHL to recent developments.
motivation: Solving linear systems is a central computational task, and quantum algorithms promise speedups. This survey aims to organize and explain the extensive algorithmic progress since HHL.
method: The paper reviews the HHL algorithm and subsequent post-HHL developments, categorizing techniques and discussing their complexities and applications.
result: Provides a structured overview of quantum linear system solvers, highlighting key algorithmic innovations and their theoretical underpinnings.
conclusion: The survey consolidates the state of the art in quantum linear system solvers, serving as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners.

title: Colloquium: Simulating non-Markovian Dynamics In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, And J. Ankerhold
abstract:
Author(s): Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, and J. Ankerhold

The dynamics of “open” quantum systems, which interact with their environments, are of paramount importance for basic research and quantum technologies alike. The field has a long and diverse history, and many different time-propagation techniques have been deployed over time and in particular in recent years, often making it difficult to relate different approaches to each other. Based on a unified framework, this Colloquium provides an overview of methods used to describe and to simulate open quantum systems in various contexts, including quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, and solid-state and many-body physics, as well as chemical physics, highlighting the commonalities and differences between them.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021002] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium provides a unified framework for simulating non-Markovian open quantum systems, covering various methods and their applications across quantum optics, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.
motivation: Open quantum systems are crucial for quantum technologies, but non-Markovian dynamics are challenging to simulate. A unified overview is needed to relate different approaches.
method: The paper reviews and categorizes time-propagation techniques for non-Markovian open quantum systems, highlighting commonalities and differences within a unified framework.
result: It presents a comprehensive overview of simulation methods, including their applicability to different physical contexts, and discusses the underlying theoretical connections.
conclusion: The unified framework aids in selecting appropriate simulation methods for specific problems, advancing the understanding and application of non-Markovian dynamics in quantum systems.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: This review explores space-time duality in quantum many-body dynamics, connecting brickwork quantum circuits to solvable dynamics and quantum computation.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult; the review aims to provide a unified pedagogical view using space-time duality.
method: The review synthesizes recent advances in discretizing time evolution on lattices, focusing on brickwork quantum circuits and their relationship to space-time duality.
result: It presents a unified framework for understanding dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems, highlighting exactly solvable models.
conclusion: Space-time duality offers a powerful perspective for studying quantum dynamics, with implications for quantum simulation and computation.

title: Colloquium: Qudits For Decomposing Multiqubit Gates And Realizing Quantum Algorithms
authors: Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, And Aleksey K. Fedorov
abstract:
Author(s): Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, and Aleksey K. Fedorov

Two-level systems—bits or qubits—are understood to generally be the most efficient primitives for information processing, classical or quantum. But this is not to say that there are no roles to be played by multilevel systems. This Colloquium surveys these possible roles for the quantum case. Here we speak of qudits:
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021003] Published Tue Jun 03, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the use of qudits (multilevel quantum systems) for decomposing multiqubit gates and implementing quantum algorithms, highlighting simplifications like the Toffoli gate with qutrits.
motivation: Qudits offer potential advantages in quantum computing, such as reduced circuit complexity and improved efficiency, but their role is not as well understood as qubits. This review aims to survey the current state and possibilities.
method: The paper provides a comprehensive survey of qudit-qubit embeddings, gate decomposition techniques, and experimental implementations, with a focus on theoretical and practical aspects.
result: The review demonstrates that qudits can simplify certain quantum gates (e.g., Toffoli) and may offer resource advantages, while also discussing challenges and current experimental progress.
conclusion: Qudits are a promising resource for quantum information processing, with potential for simplifying algorithms and reducing overhead, though further development is needed.

title: Promise Of Graph Sparsification And Decomposition For Noise Reduction In Qaoa: Analysis For Trapped-Ion Compilations
authors: Jai Moondra, Phillip C. Lotshaw, Greg Mohler, And Swati Gupta
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2185 (2026).

We develop new approximate compilation schemes that significantly reduce the expense of compiling the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving the Max-Cut problem. Our main focus is on compilation with trapped-ion simulators using Pauli-[MATH] operations and all-to-all Ising Hamiltonian [MATH] evolution generated by Molmer-Sorensen or optical dipole force interactions, though some of our results also apply to standard gate-based compilations. Our results are based on principles of graph sparsification and decomposition; the former reduces the number of edges in a graph while maintaining its cut structure, while the latter breaks a weighted graph into a small number of unweighted graphs. Though these techniques have been used as heuristics in various hybrid quantum algorithms, there have been no guarantees on their performance, to the best of our knowledge. This work provides the first provable guarantees using sparsification and decomposition to improve quantum noise resilience and reduce quantum circuit complexity. For quantum hardware that uses edge-by-edge QAOA compilations, sparsification leads to a direct reduction in circuit complexity. For trapped-ion quantum simulators implementing all-to-all [MATH] pulses, we show that for a [MATH] factor loss in the Max-Cut approximation ([MATH], our compilations improve the (worst-case) number of [MATH] pulses from [MATH] to [MATH] and the (worst-case) number of Pauli-[MATH] bit flips from [MATH] to [MATH] for [MATH]-node graphs. This is an asymptotic improvement for any constant [MATH]. We demonstrate that significant improvements to the approximation ratio are obtained using decomposition in simulated trapped-ion experiments with dephasing noise. We further present a generic argument showing that sparsification results in an exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bound in digital computing schemes based on one- and two-qubit gates, which are relevant to a wide variety of hardwares such as superconducting qubits and certain neutral atom or trapped ion setups, and more sophisticated noise models. We anticipate these approximate compilation techniques will be useful tools in a variety of future quantum computing experiments.

.
tldr: This paper provides the first provable guarantees for using graph sparsification and decomposition to reduce circuit complexity and improve noise resilience in QAOA for Max-Cut, with specific improvements for trapped-ion compilations.
motivation: QAOA compilation for Max-Cut is expensive and noise-sensitive; graph sparsification and decomposition have been used heuristically but lack theoretical guarantees. The authors aim to provide provable improvements in circuit complexity and noise resilience.
method: They develop approximate compilation schemes based on graph sparsification (reducing edges while preserving cut structure) and decomposition (breaking weighted graphs into unweighted ones), and analyze their impact on circuit complexity and fidelity for trapped-ion and gate-based implementations.
result: For trapped-ion simulators, they achieve asymptotic improvements in the number of Molmer-Sorensen pulses and Pauli-X bit flips, and demonstrate improved approximation ratios under dephasing noise. They also show exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bounds for digital schemes.
conclusion: These approximate compilation techniques offer practical benefits for near-term quantum computing, with provable guarantees that reduce circuit complexity and enhance noise resilience.

title: Entanglement Growth In The Dark Intervals Of A Locally Monitored Free-fermion Chain
authors: Giovanni Di Fresco, Youenn Le Gal, Davide Valenti, Marco Schiró, And Angelo Carollo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2183 (2026).

We consider a free fermionic chain with monitoring of the particle density on a single site of the chain and study the entanglement dynamics of quantum jump trajectories. We show that the entanglement entropy grows in time towards a stationary state which display volume law scaling of the entropy, in stark contrast with both the unitary dynamics after a local quench and the no-click limit corresponding to full post-selection. We explain the extensive entanglement growth as a consequence of the peculiar distribution of quantum jumps in time, which display superpoissonian waiting time distribution characterised by a bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals where no-clicks are detected, akin to the distribution of fluorescence light in a driven atom. We show that the presence of dark intervals is the key feature to explain the effect and that by increasing the number of sites which are monitored the volume law scaling gives away to the Zeno effect and its associated area law.

.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement growth in a free-fermion chain under local monitoring, revealing volume-law scaling due to dark intervals in quantum jumps.
motivation: Understanding how measurement-induced dynamics affect entanglement in many-body systems is crucial for quantum information and thermodynamics.
method: The authors analyze quantum jump trajectories of a free-fermion chain with local density monitoring, deriving waiting time distributions and entanglement entropy scaling.
result: They find super-Poissonian waiting times with bunching and dark intervals, leading to volume-law entanglement, contrasting with unitary and no-click limits; increasing monitored sites induces Zeno effect and area law.
conclusion: Dark intervals in monitoring are key to extensive entanglement growth, offering insights into measurement-induced phases and quantum thermodynamics.

title: On The Quantum Computational Complexity Of Classical Linear Dynamics With Geometrically Local Interactions: Dequantization And Universality
authors: Kazuki Sakamoto And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2182 (2026).

The simulation of large-scale classical systems in exponentially small space on quantum computers has gained attention. The prior work demonstrated that a quantum algorithm offers an exponential speedup over any classical algorithm in simulating classical dynamics with long-range interactions. However, many real-world classical systems, such as those arising from partial differential equations, exhibit only local interactions. The question remains whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition. In this work, we thoroughly characterize the computational complexity of simulating such geometrically local systems on quantum computers. First, we dequantize the quantum algorithm for simulating short-time (polynomial-time) dynamics of such systems. This implies that the problem of simulating this dynamics does not yield any exponential quantum advantage. Second, we show that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Third, we show that the computational complexity of simulating long-time (exponential-time) dynamics is captured by exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation. This suggests a super-polynomial time advantage when restricting the computation to polynomial-space, or an exponential space advantage otherwise. This work offers new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations, providing a pathway for achieving quantum advantage in practical problems.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the quantum computational complexity of simulating classical linear dynamics with geometrically local interactions, showing no exponential quantum advantage for short-time dynamics but potential super-polynomial advantage for long-time dynamics under space constraints.
motivation: To determine whether quantum computers can provide exponential speedup for simulating classical systems with local interactions, which are common in real-world applications like partial differential equations.
method: The authors dequantize the quantum algorithm for short-time dynamics, prove hardness results for short-time simulation, and analyze the complexity of long-time dynamics in terms of quantum complexity classes.
result: Short-time dynamics simulation is dequantized (no exponential advantage) and is as hard as polynomial-time linear-space probabilistic classical computation; long-time dynamics is captured by exponential-time polynomial-space quantum computation, suggesting super-polynomial time advantage under space restrictions.
conclusion: The work provides a thorough complexity characterization, indicating that quantum advantage for local classical dynamics may be limited to long-time simulations with space constraints, offering insights for practical quantum advantage.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: This paper constructs entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved error correction and resource efficiency.
motivation: Quantum error correction is essential for reliable quantum communication and computation, and constructing efficient quantum LDPC codes with good performance is a key challenge.
method: The authors construct EA-QC-QLDPC codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices, ensuring 4-cycle-free Tanner graphs and deriving exact rates for some families. They also propose an efficient encoding scheme and evaluate performance using QBLNMS and layered binary decoders.
result: The proposed codes show nearly an order of magnitude improvement in error-correction performance with QBLNMS decoder over depolarizing and Markovian channels, and require only one shared Bell pair for one family.
conclusion: The scalable constructions and improved decoding demonstrate practical potential for quantum communication and computing systems.

title: Atommovr: An Open-source Simulation Framework For Rearrangement In Atomic Arrays
authors: Nikhil K Harle, Bo-Yu Chen, Bob Bao, And Hannes Bernien
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2177 (2026).

The task of atom rearrangement has emerged in the last decade as a fundamental building block in the development of neutral atom-based quantum processors. As such processors grow to thousands of atoms, it becomes increasingly important to design algorithms robust to experimental sources of error. While recent progress has been made towards developing algorithms with favorable time scaling, such work has been limited to noiseless settings. Moreover, there is a lack of open-source code for reproducing and benchmarking existing algorithms. To address these deficiencies, we develop an open-source simulation framework, atommovr, and leverage it to study three distinct settings: 1) time-optimal, noiseless rearrangement, 2) noisy rearrangement under realistic error models, and 3) noiseless dual-species rearrangement. We extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, study advantageous strategies across different error regimes, and develop a novel dual-species algorithm, InsideOut, capable of avoiding 'blocked' configurations with a near-unity success rate. We hope that atommovr can serve as a common tool for the community to study rearrangement, lower the barrier to entry for new experimental groups, and stimulate progress in developing algorithms tailored to minimize atom loss in experiment.

.
tldr: This paper introduces an open-source simulation framework for atom rearrangement in neutral atom arrays, addressing time-optimal, noisy, and dual-species scenarios.
motivation: As neutral atom quantum processors scale to thousands of atoms, efficient and robust rearrangement algorithms are crucial, yet existing work lacks open-source tools and noise considerations.
method: The authors develop 'atommovr', a simulation framework, and use it to benchmark rearrangement algorithms under noiseless and noisy conditions, including a novel dual-species algorithm 'InsideOut'.
result: They extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, identify advantageous strategies across error regimes, and demonstrate that InsideOut avoids blocked configurations with near-unity success.
conclusion: The framework provides a common benchmarking tool for the community, lowering entry barriers and stimulating progress in atom rearrangement algorithms.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper presents an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits up to hundreds of qubits using tensor network contraction and Markov processes, demonstrated on QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits under noise.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is crucial for validating quantum algorithms, but scalability is limited by exponential overhead. The authors aim to extend the reach of exact sampling to larger circuits, enabling tests of quantum advantage and noise models.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction with a Markov process, where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit, allowing exact sampling from the output distribution.
result: They demonstrate exact sampling from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating depolarizing and amplitude damping noise, achieving a scale previously out of reach for exact simulation.
conclusion: This work significantly expands the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research, providing a tool to validate assumptions and conjectures at larger scales, and may inform the study of quantum advantage.

title: Quantum State Preparation With Optimal T-count
authors: David Gosset, Robin Kothari, And Kewen Wu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2168 (2026).

How many [MATH] gates are needed to approximate an arbitrary [MATH]-qubit quantum state to within error [MATH]? Improving prior work of Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, we show that the optimal asymptotic scaling is [MATH] if we allow ancilla qubits. We also show that this is the optimal [MATH]-count for implementing an arbitrary diagonal [MATH]-qubit unitary to within error [MATH]. We describe applications in which a tensor product of many single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.

.
tldr: This paper determines the optimal T-count for quantum state preparation and diagonal unitary synthesis, showing that ancilla qubits enable asymptotically optimal scaling.
motivation: The number of T gates is a critical resource for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and prior work left gaps in the optimal scaling for state preparation and diagonal unitaries.
method: The authors provide constructive algorithms using ancilla qubits and prove matching lower bounds, improving on previous work by Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer.
result: They show that the optimal T-count for approximating an arbitrary n-qubit state to error epsilon is Theta(n^2 + log(1/epsilon)) with ancillas, and similarly for diagonal unitaries, with applications to parallel synthesis of tensor products of single-qubit unitaries.
conclusion: The results settle the optimal T-count for these tasks, offering practical improvements for quantum circuit synthesis and resource estimation.

title: Geometric Speed Limit Of State Preparation And Curved Control Spaces
authors: Maximilian Goll And Robert H. Jonsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2160 (2026).

The preparation of quantum many-body systems faces the difficulty that in a realistic scenario only few control parameters of the system may be accessible. In this context, an interesting connection between the energy fluctuations during state preparation and its geometric length as measured by the Fubini-Study metric was discussed by Bukov et al. in 2019 [5]. An inspiring conjecture lower bounding the energy fluctuations by the minimal geometric length of all accessible state preparation protocols was put forward together with supporting examples and numerical evidence. However, we here show that the conjecture does not hold but can be violated if the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature, when embedded into the space of all dynamically accessible states. We illustrate this by a number of generic qubit, qutrit and harmonic oscillator systems.

.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture on geometric speed limits for state preparation by showing violations in systems with curved control spaces.
motivation: The authors aim to test a conjecture that energy fluctuations during state preparation are lower bounded by the minimal geometric length of accessible protocols, which would have implications for quantum control and thermodynamics.
method: They analyze qubit, qutrit, and harmonic oscillator systems, demonstrating that the conjecture fails when the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature.
result: They provide explicit counterexamples where the energy fluctuations are smaller than the conjectured bound, highlighting the role of curvature.
conclusion: The conjecture is not universally valid, and geometric speed limits must account for the curvature of the control space.

title: Near-Optimal Parameter Tuning Of Level-1 Qaoa For Ising Models
authors: V Vijendran, Dax Enshan Koh, Eunok Bae, Hyukjoon Kwon, Ping Koy Lam, And Syed M Assad
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2158 (2026).

The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) tackles combinatorial optimisation problems by encoding their solutions into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian prepared by a [MATH]-level parameterised circuit, with the angles tuned classically. Parameter optimisation is widely regarded as a central bottleneck, even for the shallowest circuits. Focusing on QAOA at [MATH] (QAOA[MATH]), we show that tuning the two angles [MATH] for weighted Ising models is not a black-box search but a structured signal-processing problem. We prove that the QAOA[MATH] expectation value is a partial Fourier series in [MATH] whose frequencies are determined explicitly by the problem's couplings and fields, giving instance-wise bandwidth bounds and, via the Nyquist–Shannon theorem, the sampling resolution needed to avoid the aliasing that causes coarse-grid searches to return spurious optima. We then eliminate the mixer angle analytically, computing [MATH] in closed form to reduce the search to one dimension, and apply a subdivision algorithm that locates the globally optimal [MATH] in polynomial time with a certificate of optimality when the weights are commensurable and bounded. For regular weighted graphs, we further prove the conventional wisdom that the globally optimal [MATH] concentrates near zero and coincides with the first local optimum, giving a rigorous account of the empirical success of small-angle initialisation and allowing gradient descent to replace exhaustive line searches. Validated within Recursive QAOA (RQAOA) on weighted instances of 128 and 256 qubits, our method consistently outperforms both coarsely optimised RQAOA and semidefinite programming.

.
tldr: This paper provides a rigorous analysis of QAOA parameter optimization for Ising models, showing that the expectation value is a partial Fourier series and deriving optimal sampling and initialization strategies.
motivation: Parameter optimization is a central bottleneck in QAOA, and the authors aim to show that for level-1 QAOA on weighted Ising models, the problem is structured and can be solved efficiently.
method: The authors prove that the QAOA expectation value is a partial Fourier series with frequencies determined by the problem's couplings and fields, use the Nyquist-Shannon theorem to determine sampling resolution, eliminate the mixer angle analytically, and apply a subdivision algorithm for global optimization. They also prove concentration of the optimal angle near zero for regular graphs.
result: The method outperforms coarsely optimized RQAOA and semidefinite programming on weighted instances of 128 and 256 qubits, and provides certificates of optimality for commensurable weights.
conclusion: QAOA parameter tuning is not a black-box search but a structured signal-processing problem, enabling efficient and provably optimal optimization for level-1 QAOA.

title: Sparse Identification Of Quantum Hamiltonian Dynamics Via Quantum Circuit Learning
authors: Yusei Tateyama And Yuzuru Kato
abstract: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) is a data-driven framework for estimating classical nonlinear dynamical systems from time-series data. In this approach, system dynamics is represented as a linear combination of a predefined set of basis functions, and the corresponding coefficients are sparsely estimated from observed time-series data. In this study, we propose sparse identification of quantum Hamiltonian dynamics (SIQHDy), a SINDy-inspired quantum circuit learning framework for estimating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from time-series data of quantum measurement outcomes. In SIQHDy, the unitary evolution of a quantum Hamiltonian system is expressed as a product of basis quantum circuits, and the corresponding circuit parameters are estimated through sparsity-promoting optimization. We numerically demonstrate that SIQHDy accurately reconstructs the dynamics of single-, three-, and five-spin systems, and exhibits robustness to measurement noise in the three-spin case. Furthermore, we propose an extension of SIQHDy for scenarios with limited accessible observables and evaluate its performance in identifying three-spin systems and in network-structure identification for five-spin systems.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum circuit learning framework inspired by SINDy to sparsely identify quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from measurement time-series data.
motivation: Estimating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from data is crucial for characterizing quantum systems, but existing methods may require many measurements or lack interpretability. The authors aim to adapt classical sparse identification techniques to quantum systems.
method: The method, SIQHDy, represents the unitary evolution as a product of basis quantum circuits and estimates circuit parameters via sparsity-promoting optimization, with an extension for limited observables.
result: Numerical demonstrations show accurate reconstruction of single-, three-, and five-spin systems, robustness to noise in three-spin case, and successful network-structure identification for five-spin systems.
conclusion: SIQHDy provides a promising data-driven approach for identifying quantum Hamiltonians, potentially aiding in quantum system characterization and network inference.

title: Rotation-enhanced Photonic Spin Hall Effect In A Ring Bose–Einstein Condensate
authors: Leibo Deng, Muqaddar Abbas, Ghaisud Din, Hocine Bahlouli And Yong-Hong Ma
abstract: We show that rotation can strongly amplify the photonic spin Hall effect in a ring Bose–Einstein condensate. For an incident probe beam carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM), the spin-dependent transverse shift of the reflected light is weak in the non-rotating regime but becomes strongly enhanced under rotation because rotation lifts the degeneracy of the condensate mechanical modes via Bragg scattering. The resulting mode splitting produces large photonic spin Hall shifts at ultra-low optical power, with the enhancement increasing with both the condensate winding number and the probe OAM , while remaining weakly affected by atom–atom interactions. Our findings elucidate a rotation-governed mechanism underlying spin-dependent light transport in hybrid atom–optomechanical systems, thereby highlighting its potential for applications in high-precision rotational sensing.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that rotation can strongly enhance the photonic spin Hall effect in a ring Bose-Einstein condensate, enabling large spin-dependent shifts at ultra-low optical power.
motivation: The photonic spin Hall effect is typically weak, limiting its applications. The authors aim to find a mechanism to amplify this effect for high-precision sensing.
method: They theoretically analyze a ring Bose-Einstein condensate coupled to an optical cavity, considering the effects of rotation, orbital angular momentum of the probe beam, and atom-atom interactions on the spin-dependent transverse shift.
result: Rotation lifts the degeneracy of condensate mechanical modes via Bragg scattering, leading to mode splitting and a strongly enhanced photonic spin Hall shift. The enhancement increases with winding number and probe OAM, while being weakly affected by interactions.
conclusion: The rotation-governed mechanism provides a new way to control spin-dependent light transport in hybrid atom-optomechanical systems, with potential for high-precision rotational sensing.

title: Fate Of Entanglement In Open Quantum Spin Liquid: Time Evolution Of Its Genuine Multipartite Negativity Upon Sudden Coupling To A Dissipative Bosonic Environment
authors: Federico Garcia-Gaitan And Branislav K Nikolić
abstract: Many-body entanglement properties of quantum spin liquids (QSLs), persisting at arbitrarily long distances, have been intensely explored over the past two decades, but mostly for QSLs viewed as closed quantum systems. However, in experiments and potential quantum computing applications, candidate materials for this exotic phase of quantum matter will always interact with a dissipative environment, such as the one generated by bosonic quasiparticles in solids at finite temperature. Here we investigate both the stability and spatial distribution of entanglement for the Kitaev model of QSL, which is made open by its sudden coupling to an infinite bosonic bath of Caldeira–Leggett type and then time-evolved in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. From the time-dependent density matrix of QSL subregions, we extract genuine multipartite negativity (GMN), quantum Fisher information, spin–spin correlators, and the expectation value (EV) of the Wilson loop operator. In particular, time dependence of GMN offers the most penetrating insights: (i) in the Markovian regime, it remains nonzero only in hexagonal loopy subregions of QSL (as also discovered very recently for closed QSLs), eventually vanishing on the same timescale on which the EV of the Wilson loop operator vanishes; (ii) in the non-Markovian regime with pronounced memory effects, surprisingly, GMN remains nonzero up to much higher temperatures. In addition, the non-Markovian dynamics generates emergent interactions between spins, thereby opening avenues for tailoring properties of QSL via engineering of dissipation.
tldr: This paper studies the time evolution of genuine multipartite negativity in a Kitaev quantum spin liquid coupled to a dissipative bosonic environment, revealing that non-Markovian dynamics preserves entanglement at higher temperatures.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are typically studied as closed systems, but real materials interact with environments. Understanding how entanglement in QSLs behaves under dissipation is crucial for quantum computing applications.
method: The authors model the Kitaev QSL suddenly coupled to a Caldeira-Leggett bosonic bath, then time-evolve the system in Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. They compute genuine multipartite negativity, quantum Fisher information, spin-spin correlators, and Wilson loop expectation values from the time-dependent density matrix.
result: In the Markovian regime, GMN remains nonzero only in hexagonal loopy subregions and vanishes on the same timescale as the Wilson loop. In the non-Markovian regime, GMN persists up to much higher temperatures, and emergent interactions between spins are generated.
conclusion: The findings suggest that engineering dissipation can tailor QSL properties, and non-Markovian effects can stabilize multipartite entanglement, which is relevant for quantum information processing.

title: Scalable Circuit Cutting: A Framework For Combined Gate And Wire Cuts Using Gate Groups
authors: Fiona Jiali Fr\"ohler, Yannick Stade, Christian Ufrecht, Daniel D. Scherer, Robert Wille
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum circuit cutting enables the execution of large circuits on devices with a limited number of qubits by partitioning circuits into independent subcircuits. However, this introduces a sampling overhead, which grows exponentially with the number of cuts, rendering the choice of cut placements critical for practical circuit cutting. Determining optimal cut placements remains computationally challenging, particularly as circuits grow in size. Additionally, existing circuit cutting approaches typically treat gate and wire cuts independently. Those combining both cutting approaches, however, do not take advantage of joint cutting, i.e., identifying common gate groups and cutting them jointly for a reduced overhead. This work presents a unified framework that combines gate and wire cutting within a single partitioning strategy, enabling more efficient circuit decompositions. Moreover, our approach incorporates joint cutting via a novel gate grouping technique, further reducing sampling overhead. By formulating the cut placement problem as a scalable graph partitioning task, our method efficiently identifies near-optimal cut placements for large circuits, also providing diagnostic feedback on whether circuits are suitable for cutting.
tldr: This paper presents a unified framework for quantum circuit cutting that combines gate and wire cuts with joint cutting via gate grouping, formulated as a scalable graph partitioning problem.
motivation: Quantum circuit cutting is essential for executing large circuits on limited qubit devices, but the sampling overhead grows exponentially with the number of cuts, making optimal cut placement critical yet computationally challenging.
method: The authors propose a unified partitioning strategy that integrates gate and wire cuts, and introduce a novel gate grouping technique for joint cutting to reduce overhead. The cut placement problem is formulated as a scalable graph partitioning task.
result: The method efficiently identifies near-optimal cut placements for large circuits and provides diagnostic feedback on circuit suitability for cutting, demonstrating reduced sampling overhead compared to existing approaches.
conclusion: The framework advances practical quantum circuit cutting by enabling more efficient decompositions and scalable optimization, though it is more of an algorithmic contribution than a fundamental information-theoretic result.

A key innovation is the incorporation of joint cutting via a novel gate grouping technique, which identifies common gate groups and cuts them jointly to reduce sampling overhead. The framework also provides diagnostic feedback on whether circuits are suitable for cutting, aiding practical decision-making. The work aims to overcome the limitations of existing approaches that treat gate and wire cuts independently, thereby enabling more efficient circuit decompositions for near-term quantum devices.

title: Feasibility-Preserving Quantum Search For Constrained Transportation Routing
authors: Monika Filipovska Dahye Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transportation routing problems such as the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) and the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) are characterized by strict feasibility requirements involving customer assignment and visit rules, route sequencing, and depot-return logic alongside cost minimization. Most quantum routing formulations adopt Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) encodings, where feasibility is incorporated indirectly via penalty terms in the cost Hamiltonian. While convenient for standard implementations of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), QUBO encodings allow the quantum search dynamics to allocate substantial probability to infeasible route configurations. This study develops a transportation-grounded constraint-aware Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA+) framework that embeds feasibility-preserving logic directly into the search operator. We introduce a custom mixer that functions as a quantum analogue of feasibility-preserving routing neighborhoods, using column-wise swap moves, it restricts evolution to feasible configurations while enabling structured exploration of valid routes. We compare three constraint-handling architectures: penalty-based QUBO QAOA, penalty free QAOA+ with the feasibility-preserving mixer, and a Hybrid QAOA+ combining mixer based feasibility with and penalty guidance. Results on small TSP and VRP instances show that constraint-handling architecture strongly influences feasible-route sampling, convergence behavior, and probability concentration over low-cost feasible routes. These findings position constraint-aware quantum search as a methodological extension of transportation routing search approaches, where feasibility is enforced through admissible quantum transitions rather than post-hoc penalties.
tldr: This paper proposes a feasibility-preserving QAOA+ framework for constrained transportation routing, using custom mixers to enforce feasible routes in quantum search.
motivation: Standard QUBO encodings for routing problems allow quantum search to explore infeasible configurations, reducing efficiency. The authors aim to embed feasibility directly into the quantum search operator.
method: They introduce a custom mixer that acts as a quantum analogue of feasibility-preserving routing neighborhoods, using column-wise swap moves to restrict evolution to feasible configurations. They compare penalty-based QUBO QAOA, penalty-free QAOA+ with the new mixer, and a hybrid approach.
result: On small TSP and VRP instances, the constraint-handling architecture significantly influences feasible-route sampling, convergence, and probability concentration over low-cost feasible routes.
conclusion: Constraint-aware quantum search is a promising methodological extension for transportation routing, enforcing feasibility through admissible quantum transitions rather than post-hoc penalties.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the challenge of enforcing feasibility constraints in quantum optimization algorithms for transportation routing problems, specifically the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) and Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP). Traditional QUBO formulations incorporate constraints as penalty terms in the cost Hamiltonian, which allows the quantum search to explore infeasible configurations with high probability. The authors propose a constraint-aware Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA+) framework that embeds feasibility-preserving logic directly into the mixer operator. They introduce a custom mixer that performs column-wise swap moves, acting as a quantum analogue of classical feasibility-preserving routing neighborhoods, thus restricting the evolution to the feasible subspace. The paper compares three architectures: penalty-based QUBO QAOA, penalty-free QAOA+ with the feasibility-preserving mixer, and a hybrid approach combining the mixer with penalty guidance. Experiments on small TSP and VRP instances demonstrate that the choice of constraint-handling architecture significantly impacts feasible-route sampling, convergence, and probability concentration on low-cost feasible solutions. The findings suggest that constraint-aware quantum search can be a methodological extension of classical routing search, enforcing feasibility through admissible quantum transitions rather than post-hoc penalties.

title: Large Anomalous Shifts Of Potassium-39 Feshbach Resonances
authors: Ali Zaheer, Mohammed Bouras, Krzysztof Giergiel, Rudolf Grimm, Andrei Sidorov, Peter Hannaford
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the observation of large anomalous shifts, up to +7.5 G, of the positions of the 33.6 G and 39.9 G Feshbach resonances in potassium-39 atoms confined in a 1063.9 nm optical dipole trap (ODT) at temperatures up to around 35 {\mu}K and trap depths up to about 136 {\mu}K. When the atom cloud is cooled to lower temperatures, by reducing the trap depth of the ODT, the shifts decrease proportionally with trap depth and approach zero at zero depth. We show that the large observed shifts originate from a large differential ac Stark shift between the incoming pair of potassium-39 atoms and the weakly bound Feshbach molecule, which in turn originates from an unexpectedly large dynamic polarizability of the Feshbach molecule. The polarizabilities of the Feshbach molecules extracted from the measured shifts of the 33.6 G and 39.9 G resonances are about four to seven times the sum of the polarizabilities of the two incoming potassium-39 atoms, that is, about four to seven times larger than the usual polarizability of weakly bound Feshbach molecules. The large polarizabilities of the Feshbach molecules are attributed to a near-coincidence between the frequency of the 1063.9 nm ODT laser and the frequency of a molecular transition from the last vibrational level of the lowest triplet a3{\Sigma}+u potential to a vibrational level of the excited b3{\Sigma}+g potential. Other potassium-39 Feshbach resonances we have studied exhibit a zero or very small shift, corresponding to molecular polarizabilities close to the sum of the polarizabilities of the two incoming potassium-39 atoms.
tldr: This paper reports large anomalous shifts of Feshbach resonances in potassium-39 atoms due to differential ac Stark shifts from an optical dipole trap, attributed to enhanced molecular polarizability.
motivation: Understanding and controlling Feshbach resonances is crucial for tuning interactions in ultracold atomic gases, which are used in quantum simulation and quantum information processing.
method: The authors measured the positions of Feshbach resonances in a 1063.9 nm optical dipole trap at various temperatures and trap depths, and extracted molecular polarizabilities from the observed shifts.
result: They observed shifts up to +7.5 G for two resonances, with molecular polarizabilities four to seven times larger than expected, due to a near-resonant molecular transition.
conclusion: The large shifts are explained by a differential ac Stark shift arising from enhanced polarizability of the Feshbach molecule, which is important for precise control of atomic interactions in optical traps.

The shifts are found to be proportional to the trap depth, decreasing as the trap depth is reduced and approaching zero at zero depth. The authors attribute these shifts to a large differential ac Stark shift between the incoming pair of atoms and the weakly bound Feshbach molecule, which arises from an unexpectedly large dynamic polarizability of the Feshbach molecule. The extracted molecular polarizabilities are about four to seven times larger than the sum of the polarizabilities of the two free atoms, which is unusual for weakly bound molecules. This enhancement is explained by a near-coincidence between the ODT laser frequency and a molecular transition from the last vibrational level of the lowest triplet a3Σ+u potential to a vibrational level of the excited b3Σ+g potential. Other Feshbach resonances studied show negligible shifts, consistent with molecular polarizabilities close to the sum of atomic polarizabilities.

The temperature is controlled by evaporative cooling, with temperatures up to ~35 μK and trap depths up to ~136 μK. The authors measure the resonance shifts relative to their zero-depth positions and correlate them with trap depth. To extract molecular polarizabilities, they model the differential ac Stark shift using the known atomic polarizabilities and the measured shifts, assuming a simple relationship between the shift and the difference in polarizabilities. The near-resonant molecular transition is identified by comparing the ODT laser frequency with known molecular potentials and vibrational levels, likely using theoretical calculations or spectroscopic data.

title: How Much Reconstruction Does Quantum Machine Learning Need? Late Fusion Of Independently Trained Quantum Subcircuits
authors: Prabhjot Singh, Adel N. Toosi, Rajkumar Buyya
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Circuit cutting lets a large quantum neural network (QNN) run as independent subcircuits on small devices, but rebuilding its outputs by reconstruction carries a classical sampling overhead exponential in the number of cuts - the dominant runtime cost in prior work. We ask whether, for machine-learning tasks, this step is necessary, and replace it with late fusion: each subcircuit is trained and measured independently, and a small classical head combines their outputs - a linear-cost, decision-level combination borrowed from multimodal learning. To characterize the trade-off we introduce a quantumness dial [MATH], a tunable reconstruction budget interpolating from pure fusion to full reconstruction, and a cut-entanglement diagnostic that indicates how much reconstruction a task needs (Spearman [MATH] over [MATH] runs). Across synthetic and standard datasets, independently trained late fusion matches full reconstruction accuracy within [MATH] at every point of the controlled sweep and on every classical benchmark, at exponentially lower cost; it is also markedly more robust to shot and device noise. Controlled entangled-data experiments locate the boundary where fusion must fail. We do not claim advantage over classical machine learning - consistent with recent benchmarking, quantum offers no accuracy edge on these datasets. Late fusion is thus an efficient, noise-robust, self-characterizing alternative to reconstruction for circuit-cutting QML.
tldr: This paper proposes late fusion of independently trained quantum subcircuits as a low-cost alternative to reconstruction in circuit cutting for quantum machine learning, showing comparable accuracy with exponential cost reduction.
motivation: Circuit cutting enables large quantum neural networks to run on small devices, but reconstruction overhead is exponential in cuts, dominating runtime. The authors question whether reconstruction is necessary for machine learning tasks.
method: They replace reconstruction with late fusion, where each subcircuit is trained and measured independently, and a classical head combines outputs. They introduce a quantumness dial to interpolate between fusion and reconstruction, and a cut-entanglement diagnostic to indicate reconstruction needs.
result: Late fusion matches full reconstruction accuracy within a small margin on synthetic and standard datasets at exponentially lower cost, and is more robust to noise. Controlled entangled-data experiments identify where fusion fails.
conclusion: Late fusion is an efficient, noise-robust, self-characterizing alternative to reconstruction for circuit-cutting QML, though no quantum advantage over classical ML is claimed.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the computational bottleneck in circuit cutting for quantum neural networks (QNNs), where the classical reconstruction of the full output from subcircuits incurs an exponential sampling overhead. The authors propose replacing this reconstruction step with 'late fusion', a technique borrowed from multimodal learning, where each subcircuit is trained and measured independently, and a small classical head combines their outputs. This approach reduces the cost from exponential to linear in the number of cuts. To systematically study the trade-off between fusion and reconstruction, they introduce a 'quantumness dial' Q, which interpolates between pure fusion and full reconstruction, and a 'cut-entanglement diagnostic' that predicts how much reconstruction a task requires (with a Spearman correlation of 0.59 over 104 runs). The paper presents experiments on synthetic and standard datasets, showing that late fusion matches full reconstruction accuracy within 0.04 at every point of a controlled sweep and on all classical benchmarks, while being significantly more robust to shot and device noise. They also conduct controlled entangled-data experiments to identify the boundary where fusion fails. Importantly, the authors do not claim a quantum advantage over classical machine learning, consistent with recent benchmarking, but position late fusion as an efficient, noise-robust, and self-characterizing alternative to reconstruction for circuit-cutting QML.
key_contributions: Proposes late fusion as a linear-cost alternative to exponential-cost reconstruction in circuit cutting for QNNs, achieving comparable accuracy.
Introduces a 'quantumness dial' Q, a tunable reconstruction budget that interpolates between pure fusion and full reconstruction, enabling systematic study of the trade-off.
Develops a cut-entanglement diagnostic that predicts the need for reconstruction, with a Spearman correlation of 0.59 over 104 runs.
Demonstrates through extensive experiments that late fusion matches full reconstruction accuracy within 0.04 across synthetic and standard datasets, while being more robust to noise.
Identifies the boundary where fusion fails using controlled entangled-data experiments, providing insights into when reconstruction is necessary.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is a blend of theoretical framework and empirical evaluation. The authors formalize the circuit cutting problem and introduce the quantumness dial Q, which allows them to control the amount of reconstruction performed. This dial likely interpolates between using only local measurement statistics (fusion) and using full joint statistics (reconstruction). The cut-entanglement diagnostic is a heuristic measure, possibly based on entanglement measures like negativity or mutual information across the cut, used to predict the required reconstruction budget. The experimental setup involves training QNNs on synthetic datasets (e.g., classification tasks with known structure) and standard datasets (e.g., MNIST or similar), with subcircuits trained independently and combined via a classical head. They compare late fusion against full reconstruction across various values of Q, and also test robustness to shot noise (simulated by sampling) and device noise (simulated by depolarizing or amplitude damping channels). The entangled-data experiments likely involve preparing states with controlled entanglement across the cut to see when fusion fails. The statistical analysis includes Spearman correlation and accuracy comparisons, suggesting a rigorous approach to validating their claims.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results show that late fusion achieves accuracy within 0.04 of full reconstruction across all tested scenarios, including a controlled sweep over the quantumness dial Q and on all classical benchmarks. This is a strong result, indicating that for many machine learning tasks, the exponential overhead of reconstruction is unnecessary. The robustness to noise is also notable: late fusion is markedly more robust to shot and device noise, likely because it avoids the error amplification inherent in reconstructing global correlations. The cut-entanglement diagnostic shows a Spearman correlation of 0.59, which is moderate but suggests that the diagnostic can guide the choice of reconstruction budget. The entangled-data experiments reveal a boundary where fusion fails, likely when the entanglement across the cut is high and the task requires global correlations. The paper does not report exact accuracy numbers in the abstract, but the 0.04 margin is a specific quantitative claim. The results are consistent with recent benchmarking that quantum models do not offer accuracy advantages on these datasets, but the efficiency and robustness gains are significant for practical quantum computing.

The experimental results are convincing, showing that late fusion can match reconstruction accuracy at exponentially lower cost, with improved noise robustness. title: Computation Of Thermal Entropy For The Doped Hubbard Model
authors: Yu-Feng Song, Youjin Deng, And Yuan-Yao He
abstract:

An entropy peak associated with the doping-driven quantum critical point in the 2D Hubbard model is further resolved.

method: The authors develop four complementary entropy expressions as integrals over temperature, interaction strength, and chemical potential, involving observables like energy, density, and double occupancy, and validate them with quantum Monte Carlo.
result: The schemes show excellent cross-consistency and quantitative agreement with other methods, and an entropy peak associated with the doping-driven quantum critical point is resolved.
conclusion: The framework provides a reliable and efficient way to compute thermal entropy in the Hubbard model, offering insights into quantum critical phenomena.

This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. result: It highlights key mechanisms for photodoped carrier evolution and the emergence of metastable orders such as superconducting, magnetic, and excitonic phases.
conclusion: Photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators offer a rich platform for exploring quantum metastable phases and controlling material properties.

title: Disorder-Induced Entanglement Phase Transitions In Non-Hermitian Systems With Skin Effects
authors: Kai Li, Ze-Chuan Liu, And Yong Xu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2186 (2026).

Non-Hermitian dynamics is ubiquitous in various physical systems. While recent study shows that such a dynamics leads to an area-law scaling of the entanglement entropy due to the non-Hermitian skin effects, it remains unclear how disorder changes the behavior of the entanglement entropy in a non-Hermitian system with skin effects. Here we study the dynamics of a many-body state of free fermions in the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model with open boundaries, and find that the area-law behavior of the entanglement entropy in the pristine Hatano-Nelson model develops into a logarithmic scaling for small disorder strength. As we further increase the disorder strength, the system reenters an area-law regime through an entanglement phase transition. At the critical point, the entanglement entropy exhibits a universal algebraic scaling. We further demonstrate the absence of a conformal invariance in the log-law regime by examining the subsystem entanglement entropy, the connected correlation function and the mutual information. Finally, we show the existence of disorder induced entanglement phase transitions in the Hatano-Nelson model with periodic boundaries.

.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement phase transitions in a non-Hermitian Hatano-Nelson model with disorder, showing transitions between area-law and logarithmic scaling.
motivation: To understand how disorder affects entanglement entropy in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects, which is a fundamental question in quantum many-body physics.
method: The authors numerically study the dynamics of free fermions in the Hatano-Nelson model with open and periodic boundaries, computing entanglement entropy, connected correlation functions, and mutual information for various disorder strengths.
result: They find that small disorder induces a logarithmic scaling of entanglement entropy, while stronger disorder restores area-law behavior, with a universal algebraic scaling at the critical point. They also show absence of conformal invariance in the log-law regime.
conclusion: Disorder induces entanglement phase transitions in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects, providing insights into the interplay of non-Hermiticity, disorder, and entanglement.

title: Spin-based True Random Number Generation Enabled By Voltage-amplified Quantum Fluctuations
authors: Jie Zheng, Jiyong Kang, Zheng Zhu, Di Wu, Yuesheng Li, Dongxing Yu, Jiayong Wang, Hongxing Xu And Chenglong Jia
abstract: We investigate spin quantum-fluctuation effects that originate from the Heisenberg uncertainty principle during the dynamical cycle of disentanglement, entanglement, and re-disentanglement between itinerant electrons and localized magnetic moments mediated by the s–d exchange interaction. Beyond conventional deterministic spin-transfer torque, we analyze an intrinsic mechanism that transfers spin quantum fluctuations to a nanomagnet. By extending the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation to incorporate both quantum and thermal stochastic fields, we identify a temperature regime in which quantum fluctuations dominate the magnetization dynamics. We further show that voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy exponentially amplifies spin quantum fluctuations, enabling binary readout through magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions. These findings provide a microscopic framework for fluctuation-driven spin dynamics and outline a device-level pathway toward spin-based quantum true random number generation.
tldr: This paper proposes a spin-based true random number generator exploiting quantum fluctuations amplified by voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy, modeled via a stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation.
motivation: To provide a microscopic framework for fluctuation-driven spin dynamics and a device-level pathway for quantum true random number generation, leveraging quantum fluctuations beyond thermal noise.
method: Extends the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation with quantum and thermal stochastic fields, analyzes the s-d exchange interaction's role in transferring spin quantum fluctuations to a nanomagnet, and simulates voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy amplification.
result: Identifies a temperature regime where quantum fluctuations dominate magnetization dynamics, and shows that voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy exponentially amplifies these fluctuations, enabling binary readout via magnetoresistance.
conclusion: The findings offer a device-level approach to spin-based quantum true random number generation, but the work is more applied and device-oriented, with limited direct connection to the core information-theoretic or thermodynamic principles in the research interests.

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2164 (2026).

Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) serve as important examples of ergodicity-breaking phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. In this paper, we study a two-dimensional quantum [MATH] gauge model that is dual to a two-dimensional spin-[MATH] XY model defined on bipartite graphs. We identify the exact eigenstates of the XY model with a tower structure as exact QMBS. Exploiting the duality transformation, we show that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) after the transformation are the exact QMBS of the dual [MATH] gauge model. This construction is versatile and has potential applications for finding new QMBS in other higher-dimensional models.

.
tldr: This paper constructs exact quantum many-body scars in a 2D quantum gauge model via duality to an XY model, providing a new example of ergodicity breaking in higher dimensions.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) are rare in dimensions higher than one, and this work aims to find exact QMBS in 2D gauge models, which are relevant to quantum thermodynamics and thermalization.
method: The authors study a 2D quantum gauge model dual to a spin-1/2 XY model on bipartite graphs, identify exact eigenstates with a tower structure in the XY model, and use the duality transformation to map them to QMBS in the gauge model.
result: They demonstrate that the exact QMBS of the XY and XXZ models become exact QMBS of the dual gauge model, providing a versatile construction for finding QMBS in higher-dimensional models.
conclusion: The construction offers a new route to exact QMBS in higher dimensions, potentially impacting the understanding of ergodicity breaking and thermalization in quantum many-body systems.

title: Quantum Error Management In Practice: A Cross-Stack Benchmark
authors: Daniel Sierra-Sosa, Begonya Garcia-Zapirain, Cristian Marquez, Kelly Garces
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum processors have crossed the one-hundred-qubit mark, but noise continues to limit circuit performance, while full quantum error correction remains too costly for routine use. Error suppression and mitigation therefore play an important role in extracting value from current hardware, yet independent comparisons of commercial solutions on identical workloads and devices remain scarce. We benchmark IBM Qiskit Runtime, Q-CTRL Performance Management, and Qedma QESEM on IBM Pittsburgh, a 156-qubit IBM Quantum Heron r3 processor. For Sampler workloads, we run Bernstein-Vazirani, quantum phase estimation, GHZ-state preparation, and randomized mirror circuits with up to 100 measured qubits, comparing raw execution, IBM measurement twirling, and Q-CTRL. For Estimator workloads, we measure chain-averaged magnetization and correlation observables of an eight-layer transverse-field Ising circuit at 25, 50, and 75 qubits against an exact matrix-product-state reference, comparing IBM raw execution, IBM TREX plus twirling, Q-CTRL, and QESEM. Q-CTRL produced the best results on the three structured Sampler workloads while keeping reported QPU times within the same order as the IBM configurations. Across six Ising observable and system-size cases, aggregate mean absolute error was 0.0883 for IBM raw execution, 0.0807 for IBM TREX plus twirling, 0.0285 for Q-CTRL, and 0.0188 for QESEM. Relative to raw execution, Q-CTRL and QESEM reduced aggregate error by factors of 3.10 and 4.70, respectively, while QESEM used 7.5 to 11.1 times the reported QPU time of Q-CTRL. These results show that managed error suppression and mitigation can substantially improve current hardware performance, but with distinct accuracy and execution-time tradeoffs.
tldr: This paper benchmarks quantum error suppression and mitigation techniques from IBM, Q-CTRL, and Qedma on a 156-qubit IBM processor, showing significant error reduction but with trade-offs in execution time.
motivation: Quantum processors are noisy, and full error correction is impractical; thus, error suppression and mitigation are crucial for current hardware. Independent comparisons of commercial solutions are scarce.
method: The authors benchmark three commercial error management tools (IBM Qiskit Runtime, Q-CTRL Performance Management, Qedma QESEM) on IBM Pittsburgh (156-qubit Heron r3) using Sampler and Estimator workloads, including Bernstein-Vazirani, QPE, GHZ, mirror circuits, and Ising model observables.
result: Q-CTRL performed best on structured Sampler workloads, while QESEM achieved the lowest aggregate error (0.0188) on Ising observables, reducing error by 4.70x relative to raw execution, but used 7.5-11.1x more QPU time than Q-CTRL.
conclusion: Managed error suppression and mitigation can substantially improve current hardware performance, but there are distinct accuracy and execution-time trade-offs between different tools.
